and are usually presented by the theologians who instruct the internal tribunal of the soul <note>The "internal tribunal" refers to the Court of Conscience or Penance in Catholic theology.</note>.

III. First, it appears that a possessor in good faith <term>bonæ fidei poffefforem</term> (for a possessor in bad faith is liable for his own act beyond the value of the thing itself) is not bound to any restitution if the thing has perished: because the thing itself is no longer with him, nor is there any profit from it.
<margin>Part II, Section I. Silvestro under the word Restitution, number 3, question 6. <note>referring to Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio</note></margin>
<margin>Medina on contracts, question 10. <note>Juan Medina</note></margin>

IV. Second, a possessor in good faith is bound to restore even the existing fruits of the thing. I say the fruits of the thing; for fruits of industry, even if they would not have occurred without the thing, are nonetheless not owed to the thing <note>This distinguishes between "natural" fruits, like the offspring of an animal, and "industrial" fruits produced by the possessor's labor.</note>. The cause of this obligation arises from ownership <term>dominio</term>: for he who is the owner of the thing is naturally the owner of the fruits of the thing.
<margin>Zeffi, Book II, Chapter 14. Navarro, Chapter 17, number 7. <note>Martin de Azpilcueta, known as Dr. Navarrus</note></margin>

V. Third, a possessor in good faith is bound to the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much anyway from other sources: for in this case, he is judged to be wealthier. Thus, Gaius Caesar Caligula is praised regarding the beginnings of his reign, because when he restored kingdoms to certain people, he also added the fruits of the intervening time.
<margin>Suetonius, Chapter 16. <note>Life of Caligula</note></margin>

VI. Fourth, he is not liable for those fruits which he neglected to gather: because he neither has the thing, nor anything that stands in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor has given a thing donated to him to another person, he is not bound unless he would have given just as much anyway even without this thing: for then it will be a profit to have spared his own property.

VIII. Sixth, if he has sold a thing he bought, he is not bound except perhaps to the extent that he sold it for more: but if he sold a donated thing, he is bound to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he would not have otherwise squandered.
<margin>Law "If he searches," the final section. Digest, on theft. <note>original: "L. Quivæs. §. ult. D. furti"</note></margin>
<margin>Law "If also the thing." Digest, on the petition of an inheritance.</margin>

IX. Seventh, a thing belonging to another bought in good faith must be restored, nor can the price paid out be recovered. To this rule, this exception seems to me to be added: unless the owner probably could not have recovered possession of his own thing without some expense, such as if the thing was in the hands of pirates. For then, as much as the owner would have willingly spent may be deducted. For the very possession of the fact, especially when difficult to recover, is something valuable, and in this, the owner is judged to have become wealthier after the thing was lost. And therefore, although the purchase of one's own property is not valid by ordinary law, nevertheless the Jurist Paulus says it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession which is in the hands of another should be bought. Nor do I require here that the thing be bought with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case there are those who say an action for business managed <term>negotiorum actionem</term> <gloss>a legal claim for services rendered without a mandate</gloss> arises.
<margin>Law "But even if by law." Digest, same title.</margin>

<summary>This page outlines the legal and moral obligations of a good-faith possessor regarding the restitution of property and its profits. Grotius applies principles of natural equity to determine when a possessor is considered to have gained "unjust enrichment" at the owner's expense.</summary>
<keywords>restitution, good faith, ownership, fruits of property, civil law, Caligula, maritime law, pirates, Digest of Justinian</keywords>
